title: Your service

segments.voice: Yesterday: your neighbor, the near one and the stranger, and rights owed either way. Your line was start next door.

Son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says Allah will speak words like these on the Day of Resurrection. The person is bewildered: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And the answer comes: My servant so-and-so was sick, and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. The same exchange follows about food and about water. A hospital room, a hungry stranger, a thirsty one. Khidmah.
screen: `I WAS SICK.` → `HOW COULD I VISIT YOU?` → `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Khidmah is service, the work of looking after someone else's needs. In Muslim communities you'll hear it for everything from serving tea at a gathering to running a food pantry. Why does service count as worship? That hadith does something bold. It doesn't put service next to worship. It puts Allah inside the visit. Nobody in the story is praying, and yet the sick room is where Allah is found. How is it meant to be done? In surah al-Insan, the Qur'an describes people who give food, for love of Him, to the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and who say: we feed you only for the sake of Allah; we want no reward from you and no thanks. That's a high bar, and an honest one. Service that waits for applause starts to become about the server. The same hour at a shelter can be a chore, a line on an application, or worship. The givers in al-Insan say theirs out loud: for the sake of Allah. What changes is what the hour is for. And the promise. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says Allah is in the help of His servant as long as the servant is in the help of his brother. So service isn't only something given away. In the tradition's telling, the one who serves is also being served.
screen: `KHIDMAH: LOOKING AFTER NEEDS.` · `ALLAH FOUND IN THE SICK ROOM.` · `NO REWARD, NO THANKS.` · `HELPED WHILE HELPING.`

segments.voice: Let your breath go out a little longer than it comes in, and bring to mind someone who is sick, or alone, or short of something this week, someone real if you can, without trying to fix anything yet. Let the hadith's question land: if you visited, what would you find there? If you pray, make your intention for Allah; if you don't, simply set your intention to show up without needing thanks.
Khidmah. Service to people, given for Allah's sake, without waiting for reward or thanks. Today's word.
Your line: serve. No applause needed, because the hour was never about the server. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims serve others through food pantries, hospital visits, mosque kitchens and community volunteering, describing it as khidmah, service, and as worship when done for Allah's sake; a hadith says that whoever visits the sick will find Allah there.

chat.says: Is volunteering at a shelter really worship if I'm not praying there?
options: It can be. In the hadith, Allah is found with the sick person you visit.
No. Worship only happens in prayer; service is a good habit, nothing more.
Only if people thank you for it; the reward comes from their thanks.
chat.meaning: In Sahih Muslim, had you visited the sick, you would have found Allah with him. Done for the sake of Allah, an hour of service is worship.
